what: A MicroVM Sandbox runs code the model wrote inside a tiny virtual machine with its own kernel, one per run. If the code is buggy or hostile, it can only break its own little machine, never the host or another tenant.
like: Like giving each guest their own sealed test kitchen instead of a shared one: whatever they spill stays in their room, and the room is thrown away when they leave.
why: Model-written code is untrusted code, even when your users are friendly
Containers share the host kernel; a microVM or a user-space kernel adds a real wall
Fresh per run means nothing leaks from one tenant or run to the next

steps.d: The worker asks for a sandbox for this run. A small warm pool hides boot time at peak.
Firecracker starts a guest in about 125 ms with under 5 MiB of overhead, so one VM per run is affordable.
CPU, memory and wall-clock limits stop runaway loops; no secrets are mounted inside.
All traffic goes through an egress proxy with an allowlist (package mirror, code host), so data can't be sent anywhere else.
Only stdout and chosen files come back. The VM is thrown away when the run ends.

choices.d: Containers are fast but share the host kernel. gVisor puts a user-space kernel (the Sentry) between the app and the host: VM-like isolation, process-like footprint, some syscall overhead. A microVM (Firecracker, Kata) gives each run its own kernel.
Fresh per run is safest. Reuse only within the same run or tenant, and reset the filesystem between uses.
Size the pool from peak start rate x boot time plus a margin; everything else boots on demand.

instead.why: The simple box when you don't need to show the isolation level

breaks.d: An API key mounted for convenience is one print() away from the model.
breaks.see: Keys in tool outputs or traces
breaks.fix: No secrets inside; short-lived, scoped tokens minted per run only when needed

breaks.d: Hostile code sends data out or attacks internal services.
breaks.see: Unexpected egress, calls to metadata IPs
breaks.fix: Egress proxy with an allowlist; block private ranges

breaks.d: Every run waits for a boot plus dependency install.
breaks.see: p95 start time climbs with load
breaks.fix: Warm pool, snapshots and cached dependency layers

say: Model-written code is untrusted, so each run gets its own sandbox, never shared across tenants.
For many tenants I'd use a microVM like Firecracker or gVisor, not a plain container, because containers share the host kernel.
No secrets inside, egress through an allowlist, hard limits, and the VM is destroyed at the end.

followups.a: Containers share the host kernel, so one kernel bug can let code escape. For untrusted multi-tenant code add a stronger wall: gVisor or a microVM.

followups.q: How do you keep start-up fast?
followups.a: A warm pool sized from the peak start rate, plus snapshots or cached dependency layers.

followups.q: How does code get repo access?
followups.a: A short-lived, repo-scoped token minted for the run, with egress limited to the code host.

today: Hosted agent sandboxes (E2B and others) run on Firecracker microVMs; gVisor runs as runsc under Docker and Kubernetes.

check.q: Why is a plain container weaker for untrusted code?
d: It is slower than a VM
check.why: Escapes go through the shared kernel; microVMs and gVisor put another layer in between.

check.q: What should never be inside the sandbox?
check.why: Anything inside can be read by the code the model wrote.
